title: How Sweepstakes Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain sweepstakes: their origins as marketing and lead-generation tools, the legal "no purchase necessary" requirement that distinguishes them from lotteries, and how random drawings and pre-selected winners work. They cover Reader's Digest and Publishers Clearing House history, the American Family Publishers scandal, the FTC hearings and the Deceptive Mail Prevention and Enforcement Act, odds comparisons with Powerball, sweepstakes administrators, scam warnings, the sweepstakes hobbyist subculture, and a listener mail message from James in Glasgow.
topics: Deceptive Mail Prevention and Enforcement Act

segments.title: Opening banter and the Dream Home
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about entering sweepstakes, the HGTV Dream Home giveaway, and the tax burden winners face. They plug the book chapter on The Price Is Right and a book pre-order.

segments.title: Sweepstakes origins and no purchase necessary
segments.summary: The term sweepstakes dates back centuries to pooled lottery-style betting. Modern sweepstakes differ from lotteries by having no purchase necessary, a rule that grew out of anti-lottery laws. Companies used them from the 1940s and 1950s as marketing tools and lead generators.

segments.title: Lead generation, data mining and Reader's Digest
segments.summary: Sweepstakes gave salespeople leads and now feed online data collection and third-party marketing. The hosts discuss how Reader's Digest used sweepstakes to sell subscriptions in the fifties and sixties.

segments.title: Publishers Clearing House and pre-selected winners
segments.summary: Publishers Clearing House started as a door-to-door magazine subscription business and attached sweepstakes to its mailers. The hosts describe the pre-selected winner method, where winning numbers are chosen in advance and mailed out, and how many prizes went unclaimed, leading to FTC and congressional scrutiny and second-chance drawings.

segments.title: Odds, Ed McMahon and the prize patrol
segments.summary: The hosts compare Publishers Clearing House's roughly one in six point two billion odds for its lifetime prize with Powerball's odds, and note the company's secrecy about its method. They discuss the Ed McMahon and Dick Clark association with Publishers Clearing House and the prize patrol, and the confusion with American Family Publishers.

segments.title: HGTV Dream Home drawing method
segments.summary: The HGTV Dream Home sweepstakes uses a random drawing: entries go into numbered bins, a bin is selected by lottery ball machine, and an employee blindfolded picks an entry or a computer stops a name list. The hosts note that the show's sponsorship and ad revenue motivate the giveaway.

segments.title: Fantasy Island and Bloopers detour
segments.summary: A brief digression on the Fantasy Island reboot, the Bloopers and Practical Jokes show, and the hosts' party anecdotes.

segments.title: Break and ad transition
segments.summary: The hosts tease upcoming topics and transition to a break.

segments.title: Sweepstakes today, sweepers, and scams
segments.summary: About four hundred million sweepstakes run annually, according to the hosts. They discuss sweepers, hobbyists who enter hundreds of sweepstakes daily, the Slate article on them, and brand promotions like Jeep's tiki torch hunt. The hosts also mention The Authority with Brian Arnold's sweepstakes.

segments.title: Deceptive Mail Act, scams and sweepstakes administrators
segments.summary: The hosts cover the Deceptive Mail Prevention and Enforcement Act and the elderly California man who flew to Tampa twice to claim prizes. They discuss sweepstakes administrators, scam warning signs such as up-front fees and requests for financial information, and the tens of billions lost to scams. Sandra Grauschopf is cited on sweepstakes excitement and gambling addiction.
